title: Quality control and assessment of interpreter consistency of annual land cover reference data in an operational national monitoring program
relevance: The operational blueprint for our interpretation run: LCMAP's QC design, with 2,952 pixels independently re-interpreted by a second interpreter, reporting 88% overall agreement and class-specific agreement from 46% (Disturbed) to 94% (Water), with Tree Cover among the higher-agreement classes. Gives us a defensible duplicate-interpretation fraction and a published benchmark to compare our own interpreter agreement against. Its finding that rare classes agree worse is a warning for our short-tree stratum, where interpretation will be hardest exactly where we most need it.

title: Incorporating interpreter variability into estimation of the total variance of land cover area estimates under simple random sampling
relevance: Shows how to fold interpreter disagreement into the variance of an area estimate instead of pretending the reference is exact, giving a total variance with both sampling and interpretation components. This is the mechanism that lets us report a canopy-fraction CI that honestly includes reference uncertainty - the missing piece behind finding 3, where we currently have no way to say how much of the 15-17% disagreement is irreducible. Requires duplicate interpretation of a subset, which must be designed into the ~250-point run from the start, not added later.

title: Using interpenetrating subsampling to incorporate interpreter variability into estimation of the total variance of land cover area estimates
relevance: Extends the above to a practical design: interpenetrating subsamples, where interpreters are randomly assigned overlapping subsets, so interpreter variance is estimated without duplicating every point. Directly sets the protocol if we use more than one interpreter on 250 points - it tells us how to assign points so the variance decomposition is valid. Cheaper than full double interpretation, which matters at our sample size.

title: Producing consistent visually interpreted land cover reference data: learning from feedback
relevance: Tests whether giving interpreters feedback during a campaign actually improves consistency, and reports what kinds of errors persist after training. Practical for a single-interpreter run like ours: it argues for a calibration/training block with known-answer points before the production points, and for measuring drift across the session. Also relevant to how we word the canopy-presence question, since much interpreter inconsistency traces to definition ambiguity rather than image quality.

title: Assessing interpreter's disagreements in land cover reference data collection from historical Landsat time series in Amazon
relevance: Multi-interpreter study on historical time series - our exact situation - where sets of three interpreters completely agreed on under half of pixels (39.6%) and completely disagreed on 14.8%. This is a caution against treating a single human interpretation as ground truth for the 2000s-era coarse imagery: interpreter disagreement there is the same order as our 15-17% inter-reference disagreement, so a 250-point human run may not adjudicate between C-CAP and NDVI as cleanly as we hope. Argues for recording interpreter confidence per point and reporting agreement, not just a single label.

title: Estimation of urban tree canopy cover using random point sampling and remote sensing methods
relevance: Urban-specific treatment of the point-sampling design we are about to run: how many points are needed for a target standard error on canopy fraction, and how point-sampled estimates compare against classified imagery in a city. Sets expectations for the precision a ~250-point sample can deliver - useful for checking whether our 30 vs 35 vs 38% canopy fractions are distinguishable at that sample size, which they may well not be. If not, that is a design finding we need before running the interpretation, not after.

title: A comparison of three methods for measuring local urban tree canopy cover
relevance: Compares i-Tree Canopy photo interpretation, high-resolution classification, and other local canopy estimates on the same ground, and reports that two assessors identified the same cover class at a point over 90% of the time, with no statistical difference between photo interpretation and image classification at sample sizes of 250 or more. Supplies the interpreter-agreement benchmark for urban canopy specifically, and justifies 250 as an adequate sample size for a city-level fraction. Partly contradicts our worry in finding 3: on urban canopy at a point, interpreters agree well - which shifts the blame for reference disagreement toward the products' differing canopy definitions rather than toward inherent visual ambiguity.
